title: The Mystery Revealed and a Prayer for Love
summary: Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, explains the mystery given to him by revelation: through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus. Through the church God's manifold wisdom is made known even to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms. Paul then kneels before the Father and prays that his readers will be strengthened by the Spirit, that Christ will dwell in their hearts, and that they will know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, ending with a doxology to the God who can do more than we ask or imagine.
story: Chapter 2 announced that Christ has made Jew and Gentile one new humanity. Chapter 3 begins a prayer about that (“For this reason”, v. 1), interrupts itself to explain Paul's own part in the story, and then resumes the prayer at verse 14. The digression tells how a former persecutor, the least of all the saints in his own estimate, was entrusted with announcing a secret God had kept for ages: that the nations would share fully in Israel's promises. The chapter completes the first, teaching half of the letter. Its doxology (vv. 20-21) closes that half with praise, and chapter 4 will turn to how this people should live.
historical:
Paul writes as “the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles” (v. 1). According to Acts 21 and 22, he was arrested in Jerusalem after being accused of bringing a Gentile into the temple, and he was then held in custody for several years, first in Caesarea and then in Rome. His chains were, quite literally, a result of his mission to the Gentiles. If the letter was written by Paul, it most likely comes from his house arrest in Rome, around AD 60 to 62.

The language of verses 2 and 3 (surely you have heard, as I have already written briefly) sounds as if the readers knew Paul chiefly by reputation. Scholars who see the letter as written after Paul's death take this as a sign of a later setting; those who accept Paul's authorship often see it as evidence that the letter was written for a circle of churches, including some Paul had never visited.
cultural:
The word mystery had a particular sound in the Greek world. Popular religious cults such as those at Eleusis near Athens, or the cults of Isis and Mithras, were known as mysteries: secret rites revealed only to initiates, who were forbidden to disclose them. Paul uses the word differently, drawing on its use in the Greek text of Daniel 2 for a secret of God that is revealed. For Paul a mystery is not something that stays hidden but something God kept hidden until the right time and has now made known openly, to everyone (v. 9).

Prayer in Jewish practice was usually offered standing (compare Luke 18:11, 13). To kneel, as Paul says he does in verse 14, expressed special earnestness or humility. In verses 14 and 15 there is a wordplay in Greek between Father (pater) and family (patria): every family takes its name from the Father, who stands behind all fatherhood and every people group.
literary: The chapter has an unusual shape. Verse 1 begins a sentence that breaks off; verses 2 to 13 are a long digression on Paul's ministry; and verse 14 picks up the thread with the same words, “for this reason”. The digression explains the mystery in three compound words, each beginning in Greek with the prefix for together with: fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers (v. 6). The prayer in verses 14 to 19 is a chain of requests, each building on the last: strength by the Spirit, Christ dwelling in the heart, power to grasp the dimensions of Christ's love, and finally being filled with all the fullness of God. The chapter closes with one of the New Testament's best-known doxologies, a short formal ascription of glory to God.

outline.t: The mystery revealed: Gentiles as fellow heirs
Paul's ministry and the church's witness to the powers
Paul's prayer to know the love of Christ

doctrines.note: The mystery was not discovered by human insight; it was made known by revelation, by the Spirit, to God's apostles and prophets (vv. 3, 5). God is known where he chooses to make himself known.

The church, made of Jew and Gentile together, is the means by which God's manifold wisdom is displayed to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms (v. 10). Its unity is a testimony not only to the world but to the spiritual powers.

Paul's prayer asks not for circumstances to change but for inner strength, the indwelling of Christ, and knowledge of his love. It ends in confidence that God is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine.
Paul understands his calling as a stewardship: grace given to him for the sake of others, to preach the riches of Christ to the Gentiles. The gospel is meant for every nation.

words.note: Musterion, mystery. In Paul it means a part of God's purpose that was hidden and has now been revealed. Here the mystery is specifically that the Gentiles share fully and equally in the promise in Christ (v. 6). It is an open secret, meant to be announced to everyone.

Sunkleronomos, fellow heir or co-heir. It is the first of three together words in verse 6. Gentile believers do not inherit a lesser portion; they are heirs alongside Jewish believers, sharing the same inheritance promised to Abraham.

Polupoikilos, manifold or richly varied, used of many-colored fabric or flowers. The word appears only here in the New Testament. God's wisdom is displayed in the variety of people he gathers into one church.

Patria, family or clan, a group descended from a common father. In verse 15 Paul plays on its link with pater, father: every family in heaven and on earth is named from the Father. God is not only Israel's Father but the source of every people.

christ: The chapter speaks of the mystery of Christ (v. 4) and of the unsearchable riches of Christ (v. 8). The hidden purpose of God, kept through the ages, turns out to be centered in him: in Christ Jesus the nations share Israel's promise. Through him believers have bold and confident access to God (v. 12). Paul prays that Christ will dwell in their hearts through faith, and that they will grasp the breadth, length, height, and depth of his love, a love that surpasses knowledge (vv. 17-19). The glory of God is to be seen in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations (v. 21).

hard.q: If the Old Testament already promised blessing to the nations, how was the inclusion of the Gentiles a hidden mystery?
hard.a:
God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), and the prophets spoke often of the nations coming to Israel's God (for example Isaiah 2:2-4 and 49:6). So what was hidden? Paul does not say the Gentiles' blessing was unknown; he says the mystery was not made known in other generations as it has now been revealed (v. 5). The difference lies in the how. Many readers expected Gentiles to be blessed by joining Israel, becoming Jews through circumcision and the law, or by being ruled by a restored Israel. What had not been seen was that Jew and Gentile would be joined as equals in one body, through the Messiah, without the Gentiles first becoming Jews.

Some interpreters also stress that the Old Testament promises were real but partial, like a seed whose full plant could not be seen until it grew. Either way, Paul's claim is that God's purpose was consistent all along and has now been fully revealed in Christ.

questions: Paul calls himself less than the least of all the saints, yet he is sure of his calling. How can humility and confidence go together?
What does it mean to you that the church's unity displays God's wisdom even to unseen powers?
Paul prays that you would know a love that surpasses knowledge. How do you come to know something that cannot be fully known?
